Review: Units 44–48

Units 44.1, 44.3, 44.7

"Can," "cannot," and "can't"

Use can plus the base verb to say someone is able to do something. Use cannot or the contraction can't for the negative. "Can" doesn't change for different subjects.

I can ride a bicycle. He can play guitar. I cannot sing jazz songs. I can't sing jazz songs.

can / cannot / can't

FormMeaningExample
canability, positiveI can swim.
cannot / can'tability, negativeI cannot swim. / I can't swim.

"Can" doesn't change for he, she, or it — we say "He can play," not "He cans play."

Grammar practice: complete each sentence

  1. (I / ability) I ride a bicycle.
  2. (he / ability) He play guitar.
  3. (I / inability, formal) I sing jazz songs.
  4. (I / inability, contraction) I sing jazz songs.
  5. (she / ability) She speak French.
  6. (they / inability) They come to the party.
  7. (we / ability) We finish this today.
  8. (it / inability) It fly.

Reading practice

Leo is proud of his skills. "I can ride a bicycle," he tells his friend. "I can also swim pretty well." His friend Mia laughs. "I can't ride a bicycle at all!" she admits. "But I can play the piano." Leo shakes his head. "I can't play any instrument." Their teacher joins the conversation. "Everyone can do something well," she says. "I cannot draw, but I can write stories." Mia smiles. "Maybe we can teach each other."

Check your understanding

1. Leo can ride a bicycle.

2. Mia can ride a bicycle easily.

3. Mia can play the piano.

4. Leo can play an instrument.

5. The teacher can draw well.

Units 45.1, 45.4

Using adverbs

Use an adverb to describe how an action happens. Many adverbs are formed by adding -ly to an adjective. Adverbs usually come after the verb.

I speak quietly. He speaks loudly. She walks slowly. They work carefully.

Forming adverbs

AdjectiveAdverbExample
quietquietlyspeak quietly
loudloudlyspeak loudly
slowslowlywalk slowly

Some adverbs are irregular: "good" becomes "well," not "goodly."

Grammar practice: complete each sentence

  1. quiet → adverb I speak .
  2. loud → adverb He speaks .
  3. slow → adverb She walks .
  4. careful → adverb They work .
  5. happy → adverb We laughed .
  6. quick → adverb He ran .
  7. irregular adverb (good) She sings .
  8. careful → adverb He drives .

The violinist smiles and bows gracefully.

Units 45.7, 45.8

"Good at" and "bad at"

Use good at or bad at plus a gerund (verb + -ing) or a noun to talk about skill level.

She's good at running. I am bad at making cakes. He's good at math. They are bad at cooking.

good at / bad at

PhraseMeaningExample
good atskilledgood at running
bad atnot skilledbad at cooking

After "good at" or "bad at," use a gerund (running) or a noun (math), not the base verb.

Grammar practice: complete each sentence

  1. skilled She's running.
  2. not skilled I am making cakes.
  3. skilled He's math.
  4. not skilled They are cooking.
  5. skilled We're teamwork.
  6. not skilled I'm drawing.
  7. skilled, gerund needed She's good .
  8. skilled He's chess.

Units 46.1, 46.4

Modifying adverbs

Use words like quite, very, and really before an adverb or adjective to change its strength. "Quite" is weaker; "very" and "really" are stronger.

I can ski quite well. She can ski very well. She can ski really well. He is quite tired.

quite / very / really

WordStrengthExample
quitemoderatequite well
verystrongvery well
reallystrongreally well

"Quite" can also mean "completely" before certain adjectives, like "quite right" or "quite finished."

Grammar practice: complete each sentence

  1. moderate strength I can ski well.
  2. strong She can ski well.
  3. strong, spoken style She can ski well.
  4. moderate strength He is tired.
  5. strong They are happy.
  6. strong, spoken style I'm excited about the trip.
  7. moderate strength The movie was good.
  8. strong This coffee is hot.

And Noah, your technique is very smooth." Ana smiles, feeling really proud of her progress.

Units 47.1, 47.7

"I would like" and "I want"

Use want to express a direct desire. Use would like (I'd like) for a more polite way of expressing a desire. Both are followed by "to" plus the base verb.

He wants to write a book. I would like to climb a mountain. I'd like a coffee, please. She wants to travel.

want vs. would like

PhraseToneExample
wantdirectI want to travel.
would like / I'd likepoliteI would like to travel.

"Would like" is often used when ordering food or making polite requests: "I'd like a coffee, please."

Grammar practice: complete each sentence

  1. direct desire, (he) He to write a book.
  2. polite desire, (I) I to climb a mountain.
  3. ordering politely I'd a coffee, please.
  4. direct desire, (she) She to travel.
  5. polite desire, (we) We to help.
  6. direct desire, (they) They to leave early.
  7. contraction of "would" I like to try that dish.
  8. polite desire, (he) He to ask a question.

Reading practice

At the restaurant, the waiter takes orders. "I'd like the soup, please," says Mr. Lee politely. His daughter is more direct. "I want a burger," she says. The waiter smiles. "And for you, sir?" he asks another customer. "I would like the salad, thank you," the man replies. Later, Mr. Lee's son says, "I want dessert!" His father laughs. "You should say, I would like dessert, please." The boy nods. "I'd like dessert, please," he says politely.

Check your understanding

1. Mr. Lee orders the soup.

2. His daughter says "I would like a burger."

3. The other customer orders the salad.

4. Mr. Lee's son says "I want dessert" at first.

5. The boy never learns to be more polite.

Units 48.2, 48.3

"Really" and "quite"

Use really like to show strong enthusiasm. Use quite like to show moderate interest.

I love music. I'd really like to study it this term. I like biology. I'd quite like to study it next year. I'd really like to visit Japan. I'd quite like to try sushi.

would really like / would quite like

PhraseStrengthExample
would really likestrong enthusiasmI'd really like to go.
would quite likemoderate interestI'd quite like to go.

Use "would really like" when you feel strongly, and "would quite like" when your interest is more moderate.

Grammar practice: complete each sentence

  1. strong enthusiasm I love music. I'd like to study it this term.
  2. moderate interest I like biology. I'd like to study it next year.
  3. strong enthusiasm I'd like to visit Japan.
  4. moderate interest I'd like to try sushi.
  5. strong enthusiasm She'd like to meet you.
  6. moderate interest He'd like to join the team.
  7. strong enthusiasm We'd like to see that movie.
  8. moderate interest They'd like to visit the museum.

Reading practice

At the career fair, students talk about their interests. "I love art," says Emma. "I'd really like to study painting in college." Her friend Noah shrugs. "I like science, but I'm not sure yet. I'd quite like to try engineering." A counselor overhears them. "It's great that you both have interests," she says. "Emma, since you feel so strongly, you'd really like a program focused on art. Noah, since you're still deciding, you might quite like exploring a few options first."

Check your understanding

1. Emma loves art.

2. Emma would only quite like to study painting.

3. Noah is completely certain about engineering.

4. Noah would quite like to try engineering.

5. The counselor discourages both students.

Units 48.7, 48.8

The zero article

Use no article before certain nouns when talking about a general place or institution in its typical function, like "school," "work," "home," or "church." Add the when referring to the specific building.

My daughter goes to school now. He goes to work every day. I go home at six. We go to church on Sundays.

Zero article vs. "the"

UseArticleExample
General functionzero articlego to school
Specific buildingthego to the school (to pick someone up)

"Go to the school" (with "the") usually means visiting the building itself, not attending as a student.

Grammar practice: complete each sentence

  1. general function My daughter goes to now.
  2. general function He goes to every day.
  3. general function I go at six.
  4. general function We go to on Sundays.
  5. specific building I need to go to to pick up some papers.
  6. general function She's at right now.
  7. general function They go to by train.
  8. general function He's at studying.

Units 44–48

Speaking practice

Practice speaking like in a speaking exam such as IELTS. Part 1: answer short questions about you. Part 2: prepare for one minute, then talk about a topic for one to two minutes. Part 3: act out a conversation with a partner. Try first, then open the examples.

Part 1: Interview

Answer each question in one to three sentences. Don't just say "yes" or "no" — add a reason or an extra detail.

Can / can't

1. What can you do well?

Show example answer
I can cook quite well, and I can swim. I can also speak a little Spanish.
Can / can't

2. Is there anything you can't do?

Show example answer
Yes! I can't ride a horse, and I can't sing at all.
Good at / bad at

3. What are you good at? What are you bad at?

Show example answer
I'm good at math, but I'm really bad at drawing.
Adverbs

4. How well do you speak English?

Show example answer
I speak quite well, but I speak slowly. I understand very well.
Would like

5. What would you like to learn this year?

Show example answer
I'd really like to learn to play the piano.
Want

6. What do you want to do next weekend?

Show example answer
I want to go to the beach with my friends.
Zero article

7. How do you go to work or school?

Show example answer
I go to school by bus. I usually go home at five o'clock.
Really / quite

8. Would you like to live in another country?

Show example answer
I'd quite like to live in Canada for a year, but I'd really like to visit Japan first.

Part 2: Long turn

You have one minute to prepare. You can write some notes. Then talk for one to two minutes.

Describe a skill you would like to learn.

You should say:

  • what the skill is
  • how well you can do it now
  • how you would like to learn it

and explain why you would like to learn it.

0:00 Press a button to start
Show example answer
I'd really like to learn to play the guitar. Right now, I can't play it at all. I can play a few songs on the piano, but I play very slowly. My best friend plays the guitar really well, and she's very good at teaching. I'd like to take lessons with her twice a week after work. I'd also like to watch videos online. I want to learn the guitar because I love music, and I'd like to play songs at parties with my friends. I think it's quite difficult, but I can practice every day at home.

Part 3: Role-plays

Work with a partner. Student A and Student B read only their own card. Then have the conversation.

Joining a band

Student A is the leader of a band. Student B wants to join. A asks about B's skills.

Student A

  • Ask what instrument B can play.
  • Ask how well B can play it.
  • Ask if B can sing.
  • Ask what B is good at and bad at.
  • Ask when B can practice.

Student B

  • Answer A's questions (real or imaginary).
  • Say what you'd like to do in the band.
  • Ask how often the band practices.
Useful languageCan you…?I can… quite / very / really well.I'm good at… / I'm bad at…I'd like to…How often…?
Show example dialogue

A: Hi! What instrument can you play?

B: I can play the drums.

A: How well can you play?

B: I play quite well. I practice every day.

A: Can you sing?

B: No, I can't. I'm really bad at singing!

A: That's OK. What are you good at?

B: I'm good at writing songs. I'd really like to write songs for the band.

A: Great! We practice twice a week. Can you practice on Tuesdays and Fridays?

B: Yes, I can. I finish work at five, so I can come at six.

At a café

Student A is a server. Student B is a customer. Order food and drinks politely.

Student A

  • Greet B and ask what B would like.
  • Answer B's questions about the menu.
  • Ask if B would like anything to drink.
  • Ask if B would like dessert.

Student B

  • Order food (use I'd like…).
  • Ask about one thing on the menu.
  • Order a drink.
  • Say you'd quite like dessert, but not now.
Useful languageWhat would you like?I'd like…, please.Would you like…?I want… / I'd really like…Can I have the check, please?
Show example dialogue

A: Good afternoon. What would you like?

B: I'd like the chicken sandwich, please.

A: Of course. Would you like fries with that?

B: Is the salad good?

A: Yes, it's really good. It's very fresh.

B: Then I'd like a salad, please.

A: Would you like anything to drink?

B: I'd like an orange juice.

A: And would you like dessert?

B: I'd quite like a piece of cake, but not now. Maybe later!

Writing practice

Read the task, plan your ideas, and write your text in the box. The counter shows how many words you have — it turns green when you're in the right range. Use the grammar from these units. When you finish, compare your text with the example.

Task 1: Applying for a summer job

Form50–70 words

You want a summer job at a holiday camp for kids. Write about your skills for the application form.

Write about

  • what you can and can't do
  • what you're good at
  • how well you do some things (quite well, very well)
  • why you'd like the job

Try to use

  • can / can't + base verb
  • good at / bad at + -ing
  • adverbs (well, quickly, carefully)
  • quite / very / really
0 words
Show example text (59 words)
I can swim very well, and I can play the guitar quite well. I can't cook, but I can learn quickly! I'm really good at playing games with children, and I'm good at drawing. I'm bad at singing, but the kids think it's funny. I always work carefully. I'd really like this job because I love working with kids.

Task 2: My plans and dreams

Email60–80 words

Write an email to a friend about things you want and would like to do this year.

Write about

  • one thing you really want to do
  • one thing you'd quite like to do
  • one place you would like to visit
  • why (because…)

Try to use

  • want to / would like to + base verb
  • I'd really like / I'd quite like
  • go to work / go home / go to school (no the)
0 words
Show example text (69 words)
Hi Maya, I have some big plans this year! I really want to get a new job, because I don't like going to work in my old office. I'd quite like to learn Italian, too. It's a beautiful language. And I'd really like to visit Peru in July. I'd like to see the mountains and try the food. What would you like to do this year? Talk soon, Carla
